lesson.title: Turning the Dials on Power: Sample Size, Effect Size, and Alpha
lesson.summary: Four things control how much power a test has: sample size, effect size, population variability, and the significance level, and understanding the trade-offs lets you design more sensitive studies.
lesson.body:
Four things determine the power of a test, and each one works through the same two levers you saw in the power calculation: how far apart the critical value and the true value are, and how spread out the sampling distribution is around each of them. First, sample size: increasing n shrinks the standard error, SE = sigma over the square root of n, which pulls the sampling distributions tighter around their centers and pushes the critical value closer to the null hypothesis. This is the same reason a larger sample narrows a confidence interval: smaller standard error means more precision, and more precision means a test is more likely to detect a real difference. Second, effect size: the farther the true parameter value is from the null hypothesis value, the easier it is to tell the two distributions apart, and the higher the power. A study looking for a huge effect needs less help from sample size than one looking for a subtle one. Third, population variability: less variability, a smaller sigma, means a tighter sampling distribution for the same n, which behaves just like increasing sample size, since it shrinks the standard error the same way. Fourth, the significance level alpha: a larger alpha, say 0.10 instead of 0.05, moves the critical value closer to the null hypothesis, making it easier to reject H0 whenever it is false, which raises power, but it also raises the chance of a Type I error. Power and the Type I error rate move in the same direction when alpha changes, so lowering alpha to reduce false alarms always costs some power unless something else compensates.

Return to the previous example: mu0 = 80, Ha: mu > 80, sigma = 15, alpha = 0.05, and a true mean of 88. With n = 36, the standard error was 2.5 and the power was about 0.94. Now increase the sample size to n = 64. The standard error shrinks to 15 divided by the square root of 64, which is 15/8 = 1.875. The critical value shrinks toward the null hypothesis too: 80 + 1.645(1.875) = 83.08. Standardizing against the true sampling distribution centered at 88 with standard error 1.875 gives z = (83.08 - 88) / 1.875 = -2.62, and the power is P(Z > -2.62) = 0.996. Power rose from about 94 percent to about 99.6 percent simply by increasing the sample from 36 to 64, with nothing else about the study changed.

Now hold n = 36 fixed and change alpha instead, from 0.05 down to 0.01. A stricter significance level uses a larger critical z-value, 2.326 instead of 1.645, which pushes the rejection region farther from the null hypothesis: 80 + 2.326(2.5) = 85.82. Standardizing against the true mean of 88 with standard error 2.5 gives z = (85.82 - 88) / 2.5 = -0.87, and power is P(Z > -0.87) = 0.81. Tightening alpha from 0.05 to 0.01 dropped power from about 94 percent to about 81 percent, even though nothing about the sample size or the real effect changed. This is the central trade-off in test design: you cannot simultaneously demand a very low chance of a Type I error and a very high chance of detecting real effects without paying for it somewhere, usually with a bigger sample.

When you plan a study, these four factors are the only levers available. Effect size and population variability are usually fixed by the situation you are studying, which leaves sample size and alpha as the practical design choices. That is exactly why researchers run power calculations before collecting data, to choose a sample size large enough that a test has a reasonable chance, often 80 percent or 90 percent is used as a target, of detecting an effect that actually matters.
